clue.text: Guardian puts pressure on the woman to reside in Slough

indicators.note: in an across answer, one thing on another is written before it

parts.note: first part of SHED: to slough is to shed, as a snake does its skin
the rest of SHED closes around P and HER

explanation.surface: A security guard leans on a woman to move to Slough, the unloved Berkshire town.
explanation.walkthrough: Slough is a drab commuter town west of London, so the capital S pretends to be a place; it is the verb 'to shed'.
explanation.definitionFit: A shepherd guards a flock, and figuratively any guardian or protector.

clue.text: Sun has to grovel — it makes terrible reading

parts.note: to crawl is to grovel or suck up

explanation.surface: The Sun tabloid has to toady to someone, and its pages are dreadful to read.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sun is a British tabloid newspaper, which makes 'terrible reading' look like a jibe at its content; it is bad handwriting.
explanation.definitionFit: A scrawl is messy handwriting, hard and unpleasant to read.

clue.text: House projection — decline to listen in

parts.note: the overhanging edge of a roof

explanation.surface: Notes on a house: an overhang, a falling-off, and someone listening.
explanation.walkthrough: The word's own history is here: an eavesdropper stood under the eaves where rainwater dropped, to hear what was said inside.
explanation.definitionFit: To eavesdrop is to listen in secretly on others' conversation.

clue.text: Hard member captivates English wives altogether

parts.note: first part of ARM, a limb or member
the rest of ARM closes around E

explanation.surface: A smutty image of a stiff member charming a crowd of English wives.
explanation.walkthrough: Private Eye's crossword leans on innuendo: 'member' is a limb, the arm.
explanation.definitionFit: A harem is the wives of one man, taken together.

clue.text: With right gene modification, gutless Cleverly would show some style

indicators.note: GENE is modified, its letters rearranged
Cleverly with its guts out leaves only C and Y

explanation.surface: A jibe that the Tory politician James Cleverly, lacking guts, needs gene editing to acquire any style.
explanation.walkthrough: James Cleverly is a Conservative politician; his name is only letters here.
explanation.definitionFit: Regency is a style of architecture, furniture and dress from early 19th-century Britain.

clue.text: Held back spread balls

indicators.note: to balls something up is to make a mess of it, so SPREAD is jumbled

explanation.surface: Something about balls being held back and spread, innuendo left to the reader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Balls' looks like a noun in a rude picture; it is the verb from 'balls up'.
explanation.definitionFit: To spare something is to hold it back or withhold it.

clue.text: It secures an attachment from the Daily Mirror, say — 'Conservative leader on the brink!'

indicators.note: the Daily Mirror is given as an example of a paper
the leader of Conservative is its first letter

parts.note: the lip of a cliff is its brink

explanation.surface: A newspaper headline announcing the Tory leader is about to fall.
explanation.walkthrough: The Daily Mirror is a Labour-leaning British tabloid, fitting the gloating headline. 'Leader' looks like a party boss; it takes one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A paper clip holds attached sheets together.

clue.text: To return to its original state, earth needs to enter lull

definitions.text: To return to its original state

indicators.note: to enter something is to go inside it

parts.note: first part of REST, a lull or pause
the rest of REST closes around E

explanation.surface: Environmental advice: the earth needs a pause to recover its natural state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Earth' looks like the planet in an environmental message; it is the electrical abbreviation E.
explanation.definitionFit: A defining phrase: resetting a device puts it back to its factory condition.

clue.text: Detective's last in bullying contest — "shame"

parts.note: DI is a Detective Inspector; with the 's, DI'S

indicators.note: takes the final letter of 'bullying'

explanation.surface: A detective finishes last in a bullying competition, a shameful result.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Detective's last' wants to be the E of detective; the 's belongs to DI, and 'last' works on 'bullying'.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both nouns name loss of honour and public standing.

clue.text: PC sex club dancer might make use of this T-shirt perhaps

indicators.note: a T-shirt is one example of a top

parts.words: sex club dancer might make use of this
parts.note: a lap dancer uses a customer's lap
a T-shirt is a kind of top

explanation.surface: A 'politically correct' sex club dancer might wear a T-shirt.
explanation.walkthrough: PC pretends to mean politically correct; it is a personal computer.
explanation.definitionFit: A laptop is a portable personal computer.

clue.text: Dog collar's finally done with

indicators.note: takes the final letter of 'collar'

parts.note: something over is finished, done with

explanation.surface: A dog's collar has finally been taken off for good.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is 'has': the collar's finally done with.
explanation.definitionFit: Rover is a traditional name for a dog, standing for dogs generally.

clue.text: They provide an opening for balls to pass through

definitions.text: They provide an opening for balls to pass through

parts.note: the surface hints at a body opening; the setter means the gap between two posts
innuendo aside, the balls are footballs going in to score

explanation.surface: A smutty-sounding description of something balls pass through.
explanation.walkthrough: The innuendo points at anatomy; the plain reading is a football goal, whose two posts frame the opening.
explanation.definitionFit: Goalposts stand either side of the gap a football must go through to score.

clue.text: Private Eye is onto small-time government member rejecting independent political assembly

indicators.note: MINISTER rejects the I of independent

parts.note: the magazine speaks of itself as 'we'

explanation.surface: Private Eye has rumbled a petty minister who snubs an independent assembly.
explanation.walkthrough: Private Eye is a British satirical magazine, and this crossword is in it, so the magazine's editorial 'we' is fair. 'Small-time' splits into S and T.
explanation.definitionFit: Westminster is the seat of the UK Parliament, and the name stands for Parliament itself.

clue.text: Flipping arse salt

indicators.note: to flip something is to turn it over

parts.note: an arse (a contemptible person) is a rat

explanation.surface: An expletive-laden cry about salt: 'Flipping arse!'
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' reads as a mild swear word; it is the reversal. Salt and tar are both old words for a sailor.
explanation.definitionFit: A salt, like a tar, is an experienced sailor.

clue.text: Balls displayed in automobile yard — not pleasant

parts.note: first part of GT, a gran turismo car

indicators.note: a thing displayed in a showroom sits within it

parts.note: the rest of GT closes around ROT

explanation.surface: Something rude on show in a car yard, and it isn't nice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Balls' is the exclamation meaning nonsense, not anatomy.
explanation.definitionFit: Grotty is British slang for shabby or unpleasant.

clue.text: Boris-style work event that's very unpopular with voters?

definitions.meaning: a party of the sort Boris Johnson's staff held at work
the Conservative Party, low in the polls

explanation.surface: A dig at Boris Johnson's lockdown parties, which sank him with the public.
explanation.walkthrough: Boris Johnson's Conservative government held parties at Downing Street during Covid lockdown ('Partygate'); the second reading is the Conservative Party itself, deeply unpopular at the polls.
explanation.definitionFit: A party held by Tories at work, and the Tory (Conservative) Party.

clue.text: Advisable to change topic about Nigel and Meloni finally getting together

indicators.note: TOPIC's letters are changed around
takes the final letters of 'Nigel' and 'Meloni'

parts.note: first part of POTIC, TOPIC rearranged
last letters of NigeL and MelonI
the rest of POTIC closes around LI

explanation.surface: Advice to talk about something else when Nigel Farage and Giorgia Meloni finally team up.
explanation.walkthrough: Nigel Farage leads the British party Reform UK and Giorgia Meloni is Italy's prime minister; only their final letters count.
explanation.definitionFit: Politic means prudent or wise, as in 'it seemed politic to leave'.

clue.text: 'Bollocking' or 'engaging in intercourse'

definitions.meaning: a bollocking is a severe telling-off
intercourse in its old sense of conversation

explanation.surface: Two rude-sounding words offered as alternatives.
explanation.walkthrough: A bollocking is a British slang word for a severe telling-off. 'Intercourse' is used in its old sense of conversation.
explanation.definitionFit: A talking-to is a scolding; talking to someone is engaging in intercourse (dialogue) with them.

clue.text: Artwork and its cheap reproduction

indicators.note: the letters of 'its cheap' are reproduced in a new order

explanation.surface: An original artwork and the cheap print made of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reproduction' sounds like a print of the artwork, which fits the answer's meaning too; here it reorders the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A pastiche is a work of art that imitates the style of another work or artist.

clue.text: Paper stuffed into a large dress

indicators.note: PAPER is stuffed, messed up, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Paper packed into a large dress to pad it out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stuffed' looks like padding pushed inside; it is the scrambling, and 'into' does the placing.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both are nouns for clothing in general.

clue.text: Dolly's bust: it has a number of names

definitions.text: it has a number of names

indicators.note: Dolly's is broken up and its letters rearranged

explanation.surface: Dolly Parton's famous bust has a number of nicknames.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bust' pretends to be anatomy; it means broken. At Lloyd's of London, the insurance market, the private backers who underwrite risks are called Names.
explanation.definitionFit: Lloyd's is backed by many Names, the individual investors who take on its insurance risks.

clue.text: A bit of a tit gets leg over: "Excuse not finishing"

indicators.note: PLEA does not reach its last letter

explanation.surface: An idiot sleeps with someone and offers a half-finished excuse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tit' reads as a fool and 'leg over' as sex; tit is the bird-or-breast word, and 'over' reverses PIN.
explanation.definitionFit: A nipple is a small part of a breast, slangily a tit.

clue.text: Negative Republican source that is dominating state's disgraced leader

indicators.note: the source of Republican is its first letter

explanation.surface: A gloomy Republican source dominates talk of a state's disgraced leader.
explanation.walkthrough: Manuel Noriega was the military ruler of Panama, ousted by a US invasion in 1989 and jailed for drug trafficking.
explanation.definitionFit: Noriega led Panama and ended his life disgraced and imprisoned.

clue.text: Breaking the law brings prosperity

indicators.note: 'the law' is broken up and its letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A cynical proverb: crime pays.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Breaking' sits naturally with 'the law', so the anagram signal hides inside a stock phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both mean an abundance of money and resources.

clue.text: Institutional centre that's reprehensible

definitions.note: the definition is what 'tut!' says, not a synonym for it

indicators.note: takes the middle three letters of 'Institutional'

parts.note: the three letters at the exact centre of the thirteen-letter word

explanation.surface: Something at the heart of an institution is disgraceful.
explanation.walkthrough: Institutional has thirteen letters, so its centre is insti-TUT-ional, letters six to eight.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Tut!' is the sound of disapproval, a way of saying 'that's reprehensible'.

clue.text: Nick, after unfinished article, is beat

indicators.note: THE loses its last letter
'after' means following in order

parts.note: THE, the definite article, without its E
to nick is to steal, rob

explanation.surface: Nick, trailing an incomplete article, is exhausted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nick' looks like a man's name and 'beat' like tired; nick is British slang for steal.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both nouns (or verbs) name the pulse of a heart or drum.

clue.text: One gets out of supporting hostile reformer

indicators.note: one letter leaves AGGRESSIVE

parts.note: to be pro something is to support it
AGGRESSIVE with its opening AG gone out of it
AG, which leaves: A for 'One' and G, loosely, for 'gets'

explanation.surface: Someone abandons support for a combative reformer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One gets' must supply AG to take out of AGGRESSIVE; A is one, but G for 'gets' is a stretch, so the definition and crossings do most of the work.
explanation.definitionFit: A progressive is someone who favours social or political reform.

clue.text: Sun very eager initially to finish off Cyclops?

parts.note: Sol is the sun, from Latin

indicators.note: takes the first letter of 'eager'

explanation.surface: The Sun newspaper is eager to finish off a one-eyed giant.
explanation.walkthrough: Cyclops is the one-eyed giant of myth and also the setter of this puzzle; to finish off his crossword is to solve it.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic hint by example: the Cyclops puzzle is finished off when you work out all its answers.

clue.text: BBC chief involved in erratic, mishandled case

indicators.note: ERRATIC is mishandled, its letters rearranged

parts.note: first part of CARTRIE, ERRATIC rearranged
the BBC's head is the Director-General
last letter of CARTRIE, the rearranged ERRATIC, closing around DG

explanation.walkthrough: 'Erratic' and 'mishandled' both look like anagram signals; 'erratic' is the fodder and 'mishandled' the instruction. 'Case' sounds legal but is a shell casing.
explanation.definitionFit: A cartridge is a case holding a bullet and charge, or ink, film and the like.

clue.text: The French miss being constitutional

parts.note: a miss is a young woman, a gal

explanation.surface: A French young lady is out on a walk, a constitutional.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Constitutional' tempts as a noun, a health walk; it is the adjective meaning in line with the constitution.
explanation.definitionFit: Something constitutional accords with the constitution, and so is legal.

clue.text: Labour follows its development more by accident

indicators.note: the letters of 'more by' are arranged by accident, at random

explanation.surface: A political line: the Labour Party lets things develop more by accident than design.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Labour' looks like the British political party; it is childbirth, which follows the embryo's development.
explanation.definitionFit: An embryo develops in the womb and labour, giving birth, comes after.

clue.text: Cabinet minister, evil when united with familiar old stirrer of racial divisions

parts.words: familiar old stirrer of racial divisions
parts.note: Enoch Powell, by his first name

explanation.surface: A Cabinet minister likened to Enoch Powell, the old racial agitator.
